temporal lobe seizures are preceded by a progressive increase in perfusion of the seizure focus and that this increase is inversely related to seizure interval.

temporal lobe seizures originate in a region of the brain that is characterized by progressive hypoperfusion and that epileptogenicity of the focus is a direct function of the degree of perfusion deficit.

the temporal lobe epileptic focus is characterized by a sustained decrease in cerebral blood flow (hypoperfusion) that correlates with an increased seizure frequency (decreased seizure interval) and that a sustained increase in temporal lobe cerebral blood flow (hyperemia) correlates with a decreased seizure frequency (increased seizure interval).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that temporal epileptogenicity may be a function of epileptogenic cortical perfusion.
the hypothesis that temporal epileptogenicity can be determined by the relationship between epileptic cortical perfusions and nonepileptic cortical perfusions.
the hypothesis that the epileptogenicity of temporal lobe seizures is determined by the degree of cortical hypoperfusion.

epileptogenicity in the temporal lobe is a function of temporal lobe epileptic cortical hypofusion and that the degree of hypoperfusion is inversely proportional to the frequency of seizure occurrence.
epileptic cortical hypometabolism and hypoperfusion are the result, not the cause, of temporal lobe epileptic cortical hyperexcitability.
epileptogenicity of the temporal lobe is a function of cortical perfusion.

the temporal lobe epileptic focus is a function of cortical hypoperfusion.
epileptogenicity in temporal lobe epilepsy is a function of cortical perfusion.
